newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Trade ministers told richer, safer world in reach.
newsitem.headline: Trade ministers told richer, safer world in reach.

text.p: Trade ministers and officials from 128 countries on Monday opened the first ministerial meeting of the World Trade Organisation to a ringing appeal to avoid North-South division and work for a richer, safer world.
Over the coming week, they will try to produce a blueprint for wider openings in global trade some time in the 21st century.

In a keynote speech launching the WTO meeting, Singapore's Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong told the officials that if they pushed ahead together in this direction world trade and cross-border investment would continue to expand.

"This will mean even higher living standards of living for all. Growing economic prosperity will in turn lead to greater international security and stability. This is not fantasy, but a vision within reach," he declared.

But Goh, whose booming island state has prospered as a crossroads of trade in Asia, warned the vision would quickly fade if nations failed to work together through the Geneva-based WTO and the multilateral system of rules it manages.

"Trade liberalisation requires commitment and sustained effort," he said. WTO members "will inevitably face challenges in adjusting to the realities of a rapidly evolving and more inter-dependent global economy."

Developing countries needed time to absorb the wide- ranging accords on trade in goods, services, textiles, farm produce and intellectual property reached in the 1986-93 Uruguay Round negotiations that also created the WTO, Goh said.
And he warned the big powers, who are keen to get controversial "new issues" onto the WTO agenda, not to push the emerging economies too hard.

"Realistically, global trade liberalisation has to progress in an incremental manner, even though some of us may prefer quantum leaps," the Singapore leader told his audience, which included acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky.

Barshefsky, backed by Japan and Canada, is pushing hard at the Conference, the WTO's highest authority, for a pact on ending tariffs on information technology products by the year 2000, which has only lukewarm support in Asia.
On Sunday, she said "important progress" had been made towards a deal in discussions in Singapore during the day with European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan.

Brussels differs with Washington on the product coverage of a deal, estimated to be worth up to $1 trillion a year in world trade, arguing that it is partly designed to favour U.S. products and does not fully take into account EU interests.

Goh, whose Trade and Industry Minister Yeo Cheow Tong is chairing the meeting, warned that if the WTO were to be held together "it is critical that it is not polarised by any 'North-South divide' pitting developed and developing members against each other."
And he pointed to the "new issues" of labour standards, championed by the United States, and investment, being pushed by Japan and Canada with EU support, as "especially divisive."

Emerging economies in Asia, Africa and Latin America want the ministers to focus on implementation of the Uruguay Round agreements and preparing for an already agreed batch of new tariff-reduction talks by the year 2000.

But they are fiercely resisting any inclusion of the new issues in a final Declaration, which is to set the WTO course to the end of the century, to be issued by the ministers at the end of the gathering on Friday.

Western labour unions want the WTO to link work standards and freedoms to its fair trade rules, which would mean countries violating them could face trade sanctions. The United States at present says it just wants the issue discussed.
But Prime Minister Goh appealed to the ministers to "take the broader and longer-term perspective....and display the admirable spirit of goodwill, compromise and consensus."
